section.title: The geometry of substitution
section.p: A substitution is a change of language. In single-variable calculus, we replaced x by a new variable u. In double integrals, we replace (x,y) by new variables (u,v). The new variables may straighten a slanted region, unwrap a circular region, or turn a difficult boundary into a rectangle.
But changing language changes the size of the small pieces. That is the whole issue.

subsection.title: Single-variable substitution remembered
subsection.p:
Start with the one-dimensional story. Compute \int_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx. Let x=u^2. Since x runs from 0 to 4, and we choose u\ge0, the new variable runs from u=0 \qquad\text{to}\qquad u=2. Also, dx=2u\,du. So
\int_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx \amp= \int_0^2 \sqrt{u^2}\,(2u)\,du \amp= \int_0^2 2u^2\,du \amp= 2\left[\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \amp= \frac{16}{3}.
The factor 2u did not appear by magic. It measures how much an interval in u-space is stretched when it becomes an interval in x-space.

Near a particular value u, a small interval of length \Delta u becomes an interval of length approximately \Delta x\approx \frac{dx}{du}\Delta u. For x=u^2, this says \Delta x\approx 2u\,\Delta u. Near u=2, a small u-interval is stretched by about 4. Near u=1/10, it is stretched by about 1/5.
So the one-dimensional substitution rule is really a measurement rule: \boxed{ \text{new small length in }x = \text{stretch factor}\cdot \text{old small length in }u. }

exercise.title: Why a stretch factor at all?

statement.p: We could imagine simply renaming x as u and copying the integral across unchanged. Why does honest accounting force the factor dx/du to appear, rather than letting the integrand alone carry the whole story?

hint.p: Picture two equal steps in u near u=1/10 and near u=2. Do they cover equal amounts of x?

subsection.p: In symbols, dx=\frac{dx}{du}\,du. For ordinary positive length, the scale factor is \left|\frac{dx}{du}\right|. For oriented integrals, the sign is allowed to stay. A negative derivative means the substitution reverses direction.
The same idea will guide us in the plane. The only difference is that small intervals become small parallelograms.

subsection.title: From small intervals to small parallelograms
subsection.p: Suppose a square tile in the (u,v)-plane is sent to the (x,y)-plane by T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u+2v,\;3u+v). The point (0,0) goes to (0,0). The unit step in the u-direction goes to T(1,0)-T(0,0)=(1,3). The unit step in the v-direction goes to T(0,1)-T(0,0)=(2,1). So the unit square in the (u,v)-plane becomes the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf a=(1,3), \qquad \mathbf b=(2,1).
Its signed area is \det[\mathbf a\ \mathbf b] = \begin{vmatrix} 1\amp2\\ 3\amp1 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot1-3\cdot2 = -5. The ordinary area is 5.

figure.caption: A linear change of variables sends a square to a parallelogram. The determinant measures the signed area of that parallelogram.

subsection.p: This is the two-dimensional version of the factor dx/du. A small square of area \Delta u\,\Delta v is turned into a parallelogram whose area is 5\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. The number 5 is the area scale factor.

The sign -5 also matters. It says the ordered directions have been flipped. The u-direction followed by the v-direction becomes a clockwise ordered pair in the (x,y)-plane. Ordinary area ignores that sign. Oriented area remembers it.

subsection.title: Local linearization of a coordinate map
subsection.p: The previous map was linear, so every square became a true parallelogram. Most useful coordinate maps are not linear.

For example, take T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u,\;uv). This map changes the spacing and angles of the (u,v)-grid. A rectangle with u\gt0 becomes a trapezoid: fixed u gives a vertical line and fixed v gives a line y=vx. Nonlinear maps can also produce curved edges, but this particular example has straight edges.

For a continuously differentiable map, sufficiently small images are described to first order by its derivative, as in . The two side vectors of the approximating parallelogram are the partial derivatives of T multiplied by the corresponding parameter increments.

statement.p: For a nonlinear map, a large rectangle's image can have bent sides, and its local area scale can vary across the tile. Yet near a point we use a single Jacobian determinant. In what sense does shrinking the tile rescue the parallelogram picture, and what would go wrong if we trusted that picture for a big tile?

hint.p: Think about how the curvature of the image edges compares to the side lengths as \Delta u,\Delta v shrink toward zero.

subsection.p: For T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), define T_u=(x_u,y_u), \qquad T_v=(x_v,y_v). These are the two velocity vectors of the coordinate grid: one obtained by changing u, the other by changing v.

For T(u,v)=(u,uv), we have T_u(u,v)=(1,v), \qquad T_v(u,v)=(0,u). At the point (u,v)=(2,3), these become T_u(2,3)=(1,3), \qquad T_v(2,3)=(0,2). So a tiny rectangle near (2,3), with side lengths \Delta u and \Delta v, maps approximately to the parallelogram spanned by (1,3)\Delta u \qquad\text{and}\qquad (0,2)\Delta v. The signed area scale factor is \det \begin{pmatrix} 1\amp0\\ 3\amp2 \end{pmatrix} = 2. So the image area is approximately 2\,\Delta u\,\Delta v.

figure.caption: Under T(u,v)=(u,uv), a parameter rectangle has a trapezoid image (solid outline). The derivative at (2,3) gives a nearby parallelogram (dashed outline). The difference at the upper-right corner is the product \Delta u\Delta v, drawn larger than it would be for a tiny tile.

image.shortdescription: A parameter rectangle maps to a solid-outline trapezoid; a dashed derivative parallelogram differs at its upper-right corner.

subsection.p: The upper-right corner makes the approximation error explicit: T(2+\Delta u,3+\Delta v)-T(2,3) =(\Delta u,3\Delta u+2\Delta v+\Delta u\Delta v). The derivative gives the first three terms; the remaining term is a product of two small increments.

Let us check this with a small actual rectangle: 2\le u\le2.01, \qquad 3\le v\le3.01. Since x=u, \qquad y=uv, the vertical height of the image at a fixed u is u(3.01)-u(3)=0.01u. Therefore the exact image area is
\int_{2}^{2.01} 0.01u\,du \amp= 0.01\left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_{2}^{2.01} \amp= 0.01\cdot\frac{2.01^2-2^2}{2} \amp= 0.0002005.
The local linear estimate gives 2(0.01)(0.01)=0.0002. The agreement is close because the rectangle is small.

statement.p: For a differentiable coordinate map T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), the Jacobian determinant of T is \boxed{ J_T(u,v) = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} x_u \amp x_v\\ y_u \amp y_v \end{vmatrix} = x_u y_v-x_v y_u. }

subsection.p: The notation \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} means: the determinant of the derivative matrix of the map from (u,v) to (x,y).

subsection.title: Why determinants appear
subsection.p: The determinant appears because two variables create area, and area is measured by a two-input object.

The side vectors of a tiny image tile are approximately T_u\,du \qquad\text{and}\qquad T_v\,dv. The signed area form dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of those two vectors:
(dx\wedge dy)(T_u,T_v) \amp= \begin{vmatrix} x_u \amp x_v\\ y_u \amp y_v \end{vmatrix} \amp= J_T(u,v).
So the determinant is not a random correction factor. It is the signed area of the parallelogram made by the two coordinate velocity vectors.

exercise.title: Why a determinant, not a product?

statement.p: The two coordinate velocity vectors T_u and T_v each have a length, so a tempting guess for the area factor would be the product of those lengths. Why is the determinant the right measure of how area is rescaled, while that product is not?

hint.p: Imagine the two vectors nearly parallel: their lengths stay positive, but how much area does the parallelogram they span enclose?

subsection.p:
The same fact can be written in differential form notation. In the following substitution equations, dx and dy denote the differentials of the scalar functions x(u,v) and y(u,v) on the parameter plane. Thus these are identities on one domain, not literal identifications of covectors on two different planes. Since x=x(u,v), \qquad y=y(u,v), we have dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv, and dy=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv. Then
dx\wedge dy \amp= (x_u\,du+x_v\,dv)\wedge(y_u\,du+y_v\,dv) \amp= x_u y_v\,du\wedge dv+x_v y_u\,dv\wedge du \amp= (x_u y_v-x_v y_u)\,du\wedge dv.
Thus \boxed{ dx\wedge dy = J_T(u,v)\,du\wedge dv. } This is the form version of the change in signed area.

There is one condition hidden in the phrase local linearization. The map must have a good derivative at the point. If T(u,v)=(|u|,v), then at the origin the map has a crease. Approaching from the right, the u-direction goes to (1,0). Approaching from the left, it goes to (-1,0). There is no single linear map that describes the behavior from all sides. So there is no single determinant at the origin that explains every tiny tile crossing the crease.
Away from the crease, the determinant picture works again.

For a nonlinear coordinate map, the determinant may change from point to point. That is why polar coordinates have the factor r, and spherical coordinates have the factor \rho^2\sin\phi. Before letting the scale factor vary, it is worth studying the case where it stays constant. Linear maps are the cleanest laboratory: every tiny square is stretched by the same determinant, and the curved-tile approximation becomes exact.
